sections.body_en:
The most important mitzva is the mitzva of Torah study. The Sages said that the mitzva of Torah study is equal to all the other mitzvot. They further said that the reward of the mitzva of Torah study is equal to the reward of all the mitzvot (Pe'a 1:1, and the Yerushalmi there, and the Bavli, Mo'ed Katan 9b).

There are two main reasons for the supreme standing of the mitzva of Torah study. First, through study one can know the Torah, fulfil its mitzvot and live according to its values; therefore the most basic mitzva is Torah study. This is what the Sages said (Kiddushin 40b): "Study is great, for study leads to action."

Second, the mitzva of Torah study is the most spiritual mitzva, fulfilled with the highest part of man, the intellect, and therefore its standing is above all the other mitzvot. Man is composed of body and soul, and all the practical mitzvot in the Torah are fulfilled through the body and are connected to things of this physical world. But the mitzva of Torah study is done through thought, and therefore it is the most spiritual mitzva, and through it the soul comes to full expression and elevates all deeds. Through study we rise and connect to what is beyond the world, to the world of eternity. And by the merit of Israel studying Torah day and night, connecting this world with the world of eternity, the world endures. And were the world, God forbid, idle from Torah for a single moment, it would immediately return to chaos and void, as it is said (Yirmiyahu 33:25): "Thus says the Lord: If not for My covenant day and night, I would not have set the ordinances of heaven and earth." The Sages further said (Shabbat 88a) that from the beginning of creation the earth was afraid, "for the Holy One, blessed be He, made a condition with the works of creation and said to them: If Israel accept the Torah – you will endure; and if not – I will return you to chaos and void."

Likewise the Sages said that in the order of creation the Torah preceded the world, and after the Holy One, blessed be He, created the Torah, which contains within it all the ideals and values in the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, went on to create the world in order to realise those divine ideals that are in the Torah (Pesaḥim 54a; Bereshit Rabba 1:1; 4; 10). It follows that through Torah study we connect to the spiritual dimension that is the root of this physical world. And the more we engage in Torah with diligence and depth, the more we connect to the root of life, and through this blessing is drawn into this world, and it develops and is elevated.

According to these two foundations one can understand the two components of the mitzva of Torah study. The first is knowledge of the Torah, in order to know how to live according to its guidance. The second is the study of Torah, that even a person who has already merited to know the laws of the Torah and its foundations should continue to delve into it, in order to continue drawing light and blessing into the world.

[Video]

It is a mitzva for parents to teach their children the foundations of the Torah, until they reach a level at which they can continue studying on their own. As it is said (Devarim 11:19): "And you shall teach them to your children, to speak of them." And if the parents do not know how, or are unable, to teach their children themselves, they must see to it that their children study with rabbis and teachers until they know the foundations of the Torah.

In addition to the mitzva of the parents to teach their children Torah, there is a special mitzva for the Sages of Israel to teach the people Torah, as it is said (Devarim 6:7): "And you shall teach them diligently to your children." The Sages expounded in the Sifrei that students too are called children; from here, it is a mitzva for the Torah scholars of Israel to teach students Torah.

A person whose parents and educators did not teach him Torah in his youth is obligated to study Torah on his own initiative when he grows up, with the help of rabbis and suitable books, as it is said (Devarim 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them."

One who does not review what he learned and forgets his learning transgresses the prohibition: "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things" (Devarim 4:9). If he is a Torah scholar, he is forbidden to forget the laws that he must rule on for the public, and if he is an ordinary Jew, he is forbidden to forget the guidance of the Torah for his life.1

In addition to the mitzva to know the Torah, we were commanded to engage in Torah and not to waste time in idleness: one who is not working, and is not engaged in the settlement of the world or in other mitzvot, is forbidden to waste his time in vain; rather, it is a mitzva for him to engage in Torah. As it is said (Devarim 6:7): "And you shall speak of them", and the Sages expounded (Yoma 19b): "Of them you have permission to speak, and not of other things." It is indeed permitted to relax or to go on trips in order to gather strength and enrich one's emotional world. But it is forbidden to waste time in vain, for the mitzva to study Torah is a constant mitzva, as it is said (Yehoshua 1:8): "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night."

[Video]

notes_en.en:
Torah scholars are obligated to remember the halakha in order to rule on halakha for those who ask them. As we learned from what is said (Devarim 6:7): "And you shall teach them diligently (ve-shinantam)", that it is a mitzva for Torah scholars to teach students; and they also learned from "ve-shinantam" that the learning must be sharp and well memorised (meshunan) for them, so that if they are asked, they will know immediately how to answer properly (Kiddushin 30a; Ma'amarei Re'iya, 5744 edition, pp. 198-199; Arukh Ha-shulḥan OḤ 156:2). It is possible that today, when books and databases are available, the obligation of remembering requires knowing the foundations and how one clarifies the halakha in order to answer those who ask.
According to the Semag and the Semak, the prohibition against forgetting is from the Torah, and according to the Rambam the prohibition is rabbinic, and they attached it to the verse. See the laws of Torah study in Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, in the Kuntres Aḥaron on chapter 3, p. 842. The Gra"z (Rav Shneur Zalman) wrote that only when one forgot out of laziness does one transgress the prohibition, but if one did not review because of circumstances beyond one's control, one does not transgress this prohibition. See further below, section 11, note 5, that today, when it has been permitted to write the Oral Torah in books, the stringency of the obligation to remember is not as it was in the past.

sections.title_en: Explaining the Mitzva of Knowing the Torah
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of Torah study obligates every Jew to know the foundations of the Torah, so that he will know how to conduct himself and how to relate to the events of his life according to the guidance of the Torah. Indeed, it is known that the Torah has no end or limit, and from every letter of the Torah one can learn heaps upon heaps of laws and allusions, and in every midrash of the Sages countless ideas and explanations are hidden. As it is said (Iyov 11:9): "Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea", for the root of the Torah is in eternity, and accordingly it is clear that there is no end to the depth of its ideas. But the foundations of the Torah – that is, the Written Torah, the halakha and its reasons – have a limit, and a person can study them and know them.

In the time of the Sages, they would study the foundations of the Torah until the age of twenty, and afterwards they would establish families, earn a living, and continue to review their learning and delve into it. And so it is fitting to conduct oneself today: until about the age of twenty one should study the foundations of the Torah, and afterwards begin to engage in the settlement of the world while setting fixed times for Torah. This is the mitzva incumbent upon parents – to see to it that their children study the foundations of the Torah. And one whose parents did not see to this is obligated, after he grows up, to study the foundations of the Torah himself (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:5-7). We will detail the foundations that must be studied:

The Written Torah that was given to Moshe is the foundation of everything; therefore one must study the Five Books of the Torah with a simple understanding, with a commentary, such as the commentary of Rashi, which was accepted in Israel as the most important commentary. Likewise one must study the words of the Prophets and the Writings, all of which are included in Scripture. In the time of the Sages they would begin teaching children Scripture at the age of five, and by the age of ten they would complete the Tanakh with a simple understanding (Avot 5:21).

After that one must study the foundations of halakha, giving precedence to the laws that are relevant to practice. Therefore one must study the laws of prayer, meals and blessings, Shabbat and festivals, the rule of "love your neighbour as yourself", the prohibition of causing damage, rebuke, lashon ha-ra, loans and tzedaka, returning lost property and all the other mitzvot between man and his fellow, kashrut, the synagogue, mezuza, tzitzit and tefillin, the prohibition of idolatry and what branches out from it. Likewise one must study the laws connected to the family, such as honouring parents, brit mila, the mitzva of marriage and the mitzvot that express the responsibility of spouses to each other, ḥuppa and nidda. Likewise one must study the mitzvot of the community, such as settling the Land, the mitzvot of the army, the mitzva to keep the regulations of the community, and in our days the laws of the state. These laws must be studied with the basic reasons explained in the Talmud. And the other mitzvot, which are not so relevant to practice, should be studied briefly, focusing on the general rules.

The source for giving precedence to the laws relevant to practice is the verse (Devarim 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them", that is, one must study in order to know how to keep and to do. And likewise the Sages said (Kiddushin 40b): "Study is great, for study leads to action", implying that the main thing is to study the matters that lead to action (below in note 2).

In addition, one must study the foundations of faith and ethics, because without broad and deep study of these subjects it is impossible to know properly the outlook of the Torah on life and to identify with the mitzvot of the Torah. The foundations are explained in the Tanakh and in the midrashim of the Sages cited in the Talmud and the Midrashim, and in the books of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, such as the 'Kuzari', which explains the foundations of the faith of Israel and its Torah. It is also fitting to study the books of the Maharal, which deepen thought in understanding the midrashim of the Sages in all areas of faith and ethics, and the books of Rav Kook, who broadened and deepened all areas of faith while addressing the questions of the generation. Likewise one must study books of musar, such as 'Mesillat Yesharim' by the Ramḥal and 'Ḥovot Ha-levavot' by Rabbeinu Baḥya, and every person must find the books that best suit the root of his soul. Some connect to the books of the Ramḥal, and some find an important commentary on the Torah, such as the Ramban or the 'Or Ha-ḥayim'. For some it is important to study books of Ḥasidut, and some connect to the 'Moreh Nevukhim' and the like.

In summary: every Jew must know well the foundations of practical halakha, and the foundations of faith and ethics. Only after he has studied the subjects we have enumerated will he fulfil the mitzva to study and know the Torah.

sections.title_en: The Study of Talmud and Halakha
sections.body_en:
In order to fulfil the mitzva of Torah study, which obligates us to know the Torah, one must understand the central problem. In the wake of the destruction of the Temple, the abolition of the Sanhedrin and the exile in which Israel were scattered to the four corners of the earth, the authority to decide halakha was abolished, and as the years passed, the disputes and doubts multiplied.

In the period of the Rishonim many commentaries on the Talmud were composed, but it was customary for each student to study the Talmud with the addition of one or at most two commentaries, and in this way he could cover the whole Talmud in a reasonable time, together with the halakhic rulings that emerge from it. But in the period of the Aḥaronim the books multiplied greatly, and on every sugya there are various commentaries. Likewise the halakhic rulings became long and detailed: in the period of the Rishonim they dealt with defining the general rules, whereas the Aḥaronim delved extensively into the details that stem from the words of the Rishonim, and on those details many arguments and differing opinions were stated – until the Torah literature that stands before us is a thousand times and more greater than the literature that existed in the period of the Rishonim. Since this is so, many of those who study in yeshivot tend to examine many books and analyse the various opinions closely. But in this way, the study of each sugya takes a very long time, and there is no possibility of covering all the foundations of the Torah.

Therefore, in order to know the Torah, one must study from books that summarise the foundations explained in the words of the Talmud, the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim, for only in this way is it possible to teach all students all the foundations of Torah and halakha at a reasonable level.

Some of the great Aḥaronim recommended studying for this purpose the tractates of the Talmud relevant to practice with the commentary of the Rosh, which summarises the words of the Rishonim who preceded him for halakha. But the rulings of the Rishonim after him are no longer included in it. Some recommended studying the comprehensive halakhic work 'Arba'a Turim' by Rabbi Ya'akov son of the Rosh, with the commentary 'Beit Yosef' by Rabbi Yosef Karo, which includes within it all the laws from their sources in the Talmud and the words of the Rishonim. Today the 'Beit Yosef' too does not encompass all of halakhic literature, because all the novellae, rulings and responsa that the great Aḥaronim wrote over four hundred years are not included in his book. In addition, the book 'Beit Yosef' is very long, and only a few are able to cover it and know it. Nevertheless, one must plan a programme centred around the tractates that deal with practical laws, and around the 'Shulḥan Arukh' together with the halakhic books written after it, in such a way that the practical laws are studied in detail and in depth, and the less practical laws are studied briefly. In this way most students, even those without special talent, will be able to study the foundations of the Torah, and go out to practical life equipped with good knowledge of all the practical laws. Although the vision is clear, unfortunately we still lack a book that concisely summarises the sources from Scripture and the Talmud, with the main reasonings of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim and the laws that emerge from the sugyot for practice. This is the central reason for writing the 'Peninei Halakha' series. May it be God's will that He help me to complete it properly.

Of course students are not all alike; some are more talented and some less, and each must study according to his ability. Some will study the foundations of Torah and halakha briefly and with few explanations, and some will also study the details of halakha at length, with deep and detailed explanations. The main thing is that every student, at the end of his studies, know the foundations of Torah and halakha relevant to the guidance of life.2

[Video]

notes_en.en:
The purpose of Torah study is to elevate a person and to instruct him in the way of life through fulfilling the Torah and the mitzvot; but study directed at theoretical inquiry alone is not the study that the Torah commanded. As it is said: "And the Lord commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and ordinances, that you might do them in the land into which you are crossing to possess it"; "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them"; "Only be strong and very courageous, to keep and to do according to all the Torah which Moshe My servant commanded you; turn not from it to the right or to the left, that you may succeed wherever you go. This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may keep and do according to all that is written in it, for then you shall make your way prosperous and then you shall succeed" (Devarim 4:14; ibid. 5:1; Yehoshua 1:7-8, and so in many verses). Likewise it is explained in the Mishna (Avot 4:5) that the most exalted study is the study that elevates a person until it guides him in order to do. The Sages further said that the merit of study is in that it leads to action (Kiddushin 40b), and although the Rishonim and Aḥaronim disagreed in interpreting their intention, of blessed memory, in any case it is clear that the first goal of study is to know how to act. They further said: "The purpose of wisdom is repentance and good deeds" (Berakhot 17a). Likewise the Rambam derived (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:3; Kesef Mishneh there) the obligation of Torah study from the fact that without study it is impossible to fulfil the mitzvot properly. And so Rabbi Ḥayim of Volozhin wrote in his introduction to the Gra's commentary on the Shulḥan Arukh, that the main purpose of studying the Shas is in order to arrive at practical halakha.
As a continuation of this, the poskim wrote that one should give precedence to the study of practical laws. As the Shakh wrote (YD 246:5) in the name of the Derisha, that one who can devote three hours a day to study should devote them to the study of practical halakha. And so wrote the Shelah, in tractate Shavuot, Ner Mitzva. And so wrote 'Rishon Le-Tziyon' (by the author of the holy Or Ha-ḥayim) YD 246:1, that first one must study the practical laws, "and after he knows the laws of Judaism, then it remains for him to fulfil the obligation of 'you shall meditate on it day and night'." And so wrote Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 2:1; 9, and MB 155:9: "And when he studies only a little, it is proper that his main study be in laws, so that he know how to conduct himself in practice."
In the wake of the destruction of the Temple, the abolition of the Sanhedrin and the exile in which Israel were scattered to the four corners of the earth, the authority to decide halakha was abolished and the tradition of interpreting the Torah was damaged. As the years passed, the commentaries multiplied and opinions divided into thousands of disputes and approaches, so that today it is no longer possible to cover all the words of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim written in explaining the sugyot of the Talmud and in the books of rulings and responsa. As a result, the fundamental aim of study was forgotten, and a situation arose in which many examine many commentaries on every sugya and discuss the details of reasonings, and in this way it is impossible to cover and know even a little of the foundations of Torah and halakha. Not only that, but as a result many prefer to engage in sugyot that are not relevant to practice, in which one can engage in more pilpul, since there is no obligation in them to arrive at the precise truth (Maharal, Netiv Ha-Torah 5). Already in the days of the Rishonim the great ones of Israel sought to find a solution to the problem and wrote books in which they summarised all the laws. As the Rambam wrote in the introduction to his book 'Mishneh Torah', that the aim of his book is to give those who study the possibility of learning and knowing the entire Oral Torah. This is also the aim of the book of the Semag. Rabbi Ya'akov ben Asher, who lived at the end of the period of the Rishonim, also wrote his book 'Arba'a Turim' for this aim, in which there is a summary of the opinions of the Rishonim for halakha in all areas of life. At the beginning of the period of the Aḥaronim, out of this aim, Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote his important books 'Beit Yosef' and 'Shulḥan Arukh', with the goal of collecting all the approaches of the Rishonim from all the diasporas with their reasons, and of deciding practical halakha. And still the great ones of Israel deliberated over the question of what is the good way in which one can cover the Torah as practical halakha. Some recommended the Rambam, and some recommended the Beit Yosef, and many, among them the Maharal (Netiv Ha-Torah, chapter 5), recommended studying the Shas with the commentary of the Rosh, in which the opinions of the Rishonim who preceded him are summarised with their reasons. And so wrote the Ḥavot Ya'ir 124. And so it is reported in the name of the Gra in Ma'aseh Rav 60, that he recommended reviewing the Rosh many times, and likewise the Rif, in which there are summaries of the sugyot of the Shas for halakha. He also encouraged studying the Shulḥan Arukh. In addition to striving for knowledge of the Torah as practical halakha, they warned not to sink into pilpul and fine analysis at the expense of studying the foundations of halakha, faith and ethics. As Rabbeinu Baḥya wrote in Ḥovot Ha-levavot, in the introduction and in Sha'ar Ḥeshbon Ha-nefesh, chapter 5. And so it is written in Sha'arei Kedusha by R. Ḥayim Vital, p. 42: "The custom of the early ones was that their effort was to understand the principal laws and to clarify the laws of the forbidden and the permitted, and afterwards they would engage and strive to purify their deeds and the duty of their hearts from every admixture of ulterior motives."
Although one should give precedence to the study of subjects connected to practice, and delve and be more precise in their halakhic and ethical guidance, in addition it is a mitzva to study all the foundations of the Torah, even those that do not find practical expression in daily life, and likewise it is a mitzva to know the reasons of the practical mitzvot and the values that arise from them. For the whole Torah elevates a person and straightens his mind and heart for the fulfilment of the mitzvot of the Torah and for the repair of the world. As the Sages said in the Midrash (Sifrei Ekev 48): "Lest you say: I have learned laws, that is enough for me. Therefore Scripture says: 'commandment', 'the commandment', 'all the commandment' – learn Midrash, laws and aggadot." And so wrote Rashi, Kiddushin 30a, s.v. 'eino'; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Talmud Torah 1:4; Igrot Moshe YD 2:110, that there is a mitzva to know the foundations of the entire Torah. And for this purpose the Rambam, the Semag, the Ḥinukh and others wrote their books and encompassed in them all the foundations of the Torah in brief.

sections.title_en: Dividing Study into Scripture, Mishna and Talmud
sections.body_en:
The Torah includes within it many and varied fields, and a basic question in the laws of Torah study is what the correct order of study is. In the Talmud, tractate Kiddushin (30a), a basic guideline for this is given: "Rav Safra said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya: A person should always divide his years into three: a third in Scripture, a third in Mishna, a third in Talmud."

The first part is Scripture, which includes all the books of the Tanakh. The second part is called Mishna, and in it are included the mishnayot, the baraitot and the decided laws, as well as the interpretations of the Sages and their expositions of the verses. In the past the study of the mishnayot and baraitot included within it all the rulings of the laws, but today the main study of halakha takes place in books composed after the closing of the Talmud, which include the halakhic clarifications of the Amoraim and the great Rishonim, such as the 'Shulḥan Arukh' and other halakhic books that briefly summarise the laws; therefore the main study of the part called Mishna today must be done in books of practical halakha.

The third part is called Talmud, and its meaning is understanding the reasons and reasonings of the decided laws explained in the Mishna and the Talmud, in the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim. It is also important to add that the study of the topics of faith and the secrets of the Torah is also included in the part of Talmud.

Having clarified what the three parts are, we return to the division of the hours of study.

The Rambam and the 'Shulḥan Arukh' ruled that one should divide the daily hours of study into three equal parts: a third for Scripture, a third for Mishna, that is, halakha, and a third for studying the reasons and reasonings of the halakha. And although the length of time needed for studying Tanakh is less than the time needed for studying Mishna and halakha, and the field of Mishna and halakha is smaller than the field of Talmud and inquiry, nevertheless at the beginning of study a person must divide his time among the three fields of study equally. But after he knows the Tanakh he can devote less time to it, and likewise after he knows practical halakha he can devote less time to it, and then his main study will be directed to Talmud, which is inquiry into the reasons of halakha and aggada.

And according to the Ran, the intention of the Sages is not to tell us that one must divide study into three equal parts; rather, already from the beginning of study one should devote more time to halakha than to Tanakh, and to Talmud, which is the reasons of the halakha, more time than to the study of the rulings of halakha. And the main point of the Sages' guidance is to say that every day one must engage in all three fields, but to each field one should devote fitting time according to its size and quantity.

And according to Rabbeinu Tam, one who studies the Babylonian Talmud fulfils the obligation of studying all three fields, for the Babylonian Talmud includes everything: verses from the Tanakh, mishnayot and laws are cited in it, and of course reasons and reasonings.

When we look deeper we find that there is no great dispute between the Rishonim, for all agree that at the beginning of a child's study he should study more Scripture, after that Mishna and halakha, and after that Talmud (Avot 5:21). After he knows the foundations of Scripture, Mishna, halakha and Talmud, he should invest most of his hours in delving into the part of Talmud in matters of halakha and faith. According to most of the Rishonim one must still set fixed times for reviewing Tanakh and halakha, whereas according to Rabbeinu Tam the study of the Babylonian Talmud, which includes everything, suffices, provided that within his study he takes note of the halakhic conclusion.

Some follow the practice of Rabbeinu Tam (Rema and Shakh YD 246:5). And many hold that it is proper to devote a special time every day both to Tanakh and to halakha, and so ruled the Rambam (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:11), the 'Shulḥan Arukh' (YD 246:4), the Baḥ and the 'Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav' (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 2:2).

[Video]

A question of principle is what a person should do when two possibilities stand before him: to study Torah or to fulfil another mitzva. On the one hand, the mitzva of Torah study is the most important of all the mitzvot; on the other hand, the whole aim of the Torah is to guide our lives in this world, and it is for this that all the mitzvot were given. The Sages said that the purpose of wisdom and study is repentance and good deeds, and if he does not intend to fulfil the mitzvot written in the Torah, for what purpose did he study? The Sages also said that for one who studies and does not fulfil the mitzvot it would have been better not to study at all, and the Torah becomes for him a deadly poison, and his punishment is greater than the punishment of one who neither studied nor fulfils mitzvot (Berakhot 17a; Yoma 72b).

The basic rule in this matter is that one should interrupt Torah study in order to fulfil a mitzva that cannot be done by others, and it is not proper to interrupt Torah study in order to fulfil a mitzva that can be done by others (Mo'ed Katan 9a). We will explain further:

Every mitzva that according to the Torah carries a personal obligation to fulfil it – even one who is engaged in Torah study must stop his study in order to fulfil it. For example, those who study Torah must stop their study in order to fulfil the mitzva of putting on tefillin, Keri'at Shema, taking the lulav and the like. Likewise, when parents need personal help from their son, he must stop his study and help them.

But there are mitzvot that are not incumbent upon every person personally, and regarding them the law depends on whether there is someone else who can fulfil them. For example, when a loan must be given to a friend, and there is no other person there who can lend to him, the one studying must stop his study and give him the loan. Likewise, when one must participate in the funeral of the deceased, and there are not enough people there to participate in the funeral and honour the deceased properly, he must stop his study and accompany the deceased. But if there are enough people there, it is better that he continue studying.

The same law applies to one who needs to ask for help from his friend: first he should turn to someone who is not studying Torah at that time, so as not to cause an interruption of study, and only if he did not find such a person should he turn to those studying Torah.

[Video]

sections.title_en: The Mitzva of Knowing the Torah versus Other Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
On top of the well-known rule that one interrupts Torah for a mitzva that others cannot fulfil, an important foundation must be added. As is known, the mitzva of Torah study is divided into two parts: one, the mitzva to know the foundations of the Torah; and the second, that even one who already knows the foundations of the Torah should continue to delve into the Torah. The mitzva of knowing the Torah is fulfilled mainly by young boys who study the foundations of the Torah, and likewise by ba'alei teshuva who did not merit to study Torah in their youth.

Everything that was said, that one sets aside Torah study in order to fulfil mitzvot that others cannot fulfil, is on condition that the mitzva of knowing the Torah not be harmed. But when fulfilling a certain mitzva will cause the nullification of the mitzva of knowing the Torah – that is, that by fulfilling it that Jew will not know the foundations of the Torah, or his connection to the Torah will be significantly harmed – then the mitzva of study prevails, and the other mitzva is set aside before it.

Therefore, when people come to yeshivot and ask the boys to volunteer for all kinds of needs of mitzva – to help in hospitals, to help the elderly, to volunteer for the civil guard and for Magen David Adom; and also bereaved families ask for young men to complete a minyan for them and to go with the families on the thirtieth day and on the anniversary to the grave of their loved one – the heads of the yeshivot and the teachers must examine the situation well. If they see that as a result of these volunteer activities the young men will in the end not know the foundations of the Torah, or their connection to the Torah will be significantly harmed, they must instruct the students to continue their study and not to volunteer, and this even though no other people will be found to volunteer in their place.

All this is said regarding voluntary mitzvot, which are not personally incumbent upon each and every one of Israel. But the mitzvot incumbent upon every person of Israel override Torah study. Therefore one interrupts Torah in order to put on tefillin on weekdays, to recite Birkat Ha-mazon after eating, to hear the shofar on Rosh Ha-shana, to take the lulav on Sukkot, and to eat matza on Pesaḥ. For the fulfilment of the mitzvot incumbent upon every person of Israel does not take so much time, and there is no problem in fulfilling them and at the same time studying the Torah and knowing it (based on Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:1, and the Kuntres Aḥaron there).

[Video]

In the previous section we learned a basic rule: although fulfilling the mitzvot overrides the mitzva of Torah study, when fulfilling the mitzva will cause a person not to know the foundations of the Torah, the mitzva of study prevails, for every Jew is obligated to know the foundations of the Torah.

This is the main reason for postponing the age of marriage. Were it not so, one would have to marry at the age of thirteen, since at the age of thirteen a son becomes obligated in the mitzvot, and there is a mitzva to marry. But since at these ages the boy must study the foundations of the Torah, and thereby build his personality, the age of marriage was postponed. (Today further reasons have been added for postponing the age of marriage, as explained in note 3.)

In order to reach the basic level of knowledge of the Torah, the Sages guided us in tractate Avot (5:21) to study Torah until the age of twenty. By the age of ten they would finish the study of Scripture, by the age of fifteen they finished the study of Mishna and halakha, and by the age of twenty they finished the study of the reasons of halakha and the ideas of faith and ethics. Therefore the Sages taught that between the ages of eighteen and twenty it is fitting to marry, for then the young man is already close to knowing the foundations of the Torah, and he can leave the beit midrash and take upon himself the yoke of the family. And even if he marries earlier, right at the age of eighteen, he will be able to complete his course of study, since the yoke of the family in the first two years is not so burdensome. In any case, by the age of twenty he must marry, and he may not postpone his marriage in order to continue rising in Torah, for only the mitzva of knowing the foundations of the Torah overrides marriage, and not the mitzva of Torah study.

Today, due to various factors, the age of marriage is delayed by several years. One of the reasons for this is that in the wake of the compositions of the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim, the halakhic sugyot multiplied and became more detailed, and the topics of thought in the face of the challenges of our generation also became more complex, and in practice it takes longer today to study the foundations of the Torah and to understand them in fitting depth. Therefore the recommendation for most young men is to delay marriage until after the age of twenty, but not later than the age of twenty-four (Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 5:7-9, note 12).3

[Video]

notes_en.en:
A further reason for postponing the age of marriage is the need to prepare for the yoke of earning a living. Today the professional preparation for a respectable livelihood takes a long time, each person according to the profession that suits him, and it is not possible to bring forward the age of marriage as in the time of the Sages, because early marriage could prevent young people from acquiring a suitable profession and afterwards supporting their families respectably. Unfortunately, Torah study in the period of youth is also not yet carried out with the required efficiency. All this causes marriage to be delayed beyond the age of twenty for the great majority of young men. A further reason for postponing the age of marriage is the mitzva to serve in the army to defend the people and the Land. A further reason: the complexity of life in the modern era presents a couple with more trials than in the past, and in order to cope with them more maturity and responsibility are needed. These topics are explained at length in Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 5:7-9; 12.
I wrote according to the general guidance, that one who already knows the foundations of the Torah is commanded to marry and not to postpone his marriage further. It is indeed ruled in SA EH 1:2 that one who fears that marriage will cause him to neglect Torah, and therefore does not marry, bears no sin, and so did Ben Azzai. Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (Hilkhot Talmud Torah, chapter 3, at the beginning of note 1 in the Kuntres Aḥaron) explained that Ben Azzai feared that he would forget the Torah, that is, that marriage would harm the mitzva of knowing the Torah, and on this basis he ruled for himself a permission not to marry. But the opinion of the Sages is that one need not fear this, and one must marry and continue to set several hours for reviewing one's learning. And even if, because of the constraints of his livelihood, he is not able to review properly, he bears no sin, since he forgot under duress. There is a further explanation of Ben Azzai's practice: that because of the intensity of his attachment and diligence in Torah he could not emotionally free himself for the bond of marriage, which must be based on attentiveness and love, and therefore, under duress, he could not marry (Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 5, note 1).

sections.title_en: How Many Hours a Day Should One Devote to Study?
sections.body_en:
Until now we have dealt with the study that every Jew must study in his childhood and youth, a study that continues, according to the guidance of the Sages, until about the age of twenty. Now we will deal with the question of how many hours an adult must devote to Torah study on weekdays.

Apparently there are different and contradictory guidelines in the words of the Sages. On the one hand there are guidelines establishing that the main part of the day must be directed to study, as they said: "Make your Torah fixed and your work occasional." And likewise Rabbi Yishmael said that one should make the Torah fixed, that is, study most of the day, and only a little of the day engage in work and livelihood (Berakhot 35b).

On the other hand we find many sources in the words of the Sages from which it clearly appears that most of the day is devoted to work. For example, in tractate Berakhot (4b) the life of a Jew is described who comes from the field in the evening, and then studies for a while.

The explanation of this is that one who is suited to be a Torah scholar, both in his talent and in his character and desire, bears the responsibility to make his Torah fixed and his work occasional. But one who finds himself more suited to engage in the settlement of the world – it is better that he devote more time to work, and he may work most of his day and earn a respectable living. And he should be careful to set fixed times for Torah, so that he constantly reviews the foundations of the Torah that he learned, and even broadens and deepens a little in the Torah (Orot Ha-Torah 9:6, based on Tosafot Yeshanim, Yoma 85b).4 And such a person, if he was very busy on a particular day, should try to study at least one chapter in the morning and one chapter in the evening. And if he does not have time even for this, he fulfils his obligation in a time of pressing need with Keri'at Shema of the morning and evening (Menaḥot 99b, Rema and Shakh YD 246:1). On the contrary, it is fitting that such a person earn a great deal, so that he can support the poor and maintain those who study Torah (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:4).

However, even one who finds himself suited by his talents to one of the various fields of work must be careful about two principles. The first: to review his learning so as not to forget the foundations of the Torah. The second: not to waste his time in vain with too much entertainment. For as long as he is working and engaged in the settlement of the world this is not neglect of Torah, but if he wastes his time in idleness beyond what he needs to rest and relax, he transgresses the prohibition of neglecting Torah. As the Sages said (Yoma 19b): "'And you shall speak of them' – of them and not of other things."

It is also important to mention that the poskim wrote that one who can devote only a few hours a day to study should not study only Gemara in them; rather, the main thing is that he study in them halakha with its reasons and sources, and likewise ideas of thought whose foundation is in the midrashim of the Sages (Derisha, Shakh, Taz on YD 246, and Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 2:9).

A person who does not need to work a full-time job and has free hours, and likewise one who has retired, is commanded not to waste his time in vain, and together with all the good things he does, he should devote several good hours every day to the study of Torah.

[Video]

notes_en.en: The Sages said (Avot 2:2): "Torah study is good together with derekh eretz (work to earn a living)… and any Torah that is not accompanied by work will in the end come to nothing…" It is explained in Tosafot Yeshanim, Yoma 85b, that according to Rabbeinu Tam, the meaning is that derekh eretz is primary and Torah study secondary. On the other hand, according to R. Elḥanan the Torah is primary, and the proof is that later in the mishna they said "and any Torah that is not accompanied by work will in the end come to nothing", implying that the Torah is primary, but that some work is needed together with it. And so it is explained in the Talmud (Berakhot 35b): "Come and see that the later generations are not like the earlier generations. The earlier generations made their Torah fixed and their work occasional – both this and that endured in their hands; the later generations, who made their work fixed and their Torah occasional – neither this nor that endured in their hands." Our master Rav Kook wrote about this (Orot Ha-Torah 9:6): "The matter depends on the character and nature of the soul of each and every one."

sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to increase Torah study on Sabbaths and festivals, as the Sages said (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:3): "Sabbaths and festivals were given only in order to engage in words of Torah on them." This instruction is especially important for people who are engaged in the settlement of the world. And so the Sages said: "The Torah said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, when Israel enter the Land, this one will run to his vineyard and that one will run to his field, and what will become of me? He said to her: I have a partner whom I will pair with you, and Shabbat is its name, for they are idle from their work and can engage in you" (Tur OḤ 290).

There are two foundations for this: one, the mitzva of Torah study, which obligates one to study much Torah every day; but on weekdays, since people are occupied with earning a living, they make do with setting fixed times for Torah during the day and at night (Rambam, ibid. 1:8; 3:13). But on Sabbaths and festivals, when a person is free from his work, the mitzva of Torah study returns to its place in its full force. For this purpose Sabbaths and festivals were given to Israel, so that they would be free from their work and could engage in Torah.

The second foundation: the Sabbaths and festivals are holy days that were given to Israel so that they would rise on them in the levels of Torah, and through them illuminate the weekdays. Shabbat is intended to illuminate and elevate the six weekdays every week, and each of the festivals is intended to shine its special light over the whole year. Therefore Moshe our teacher instituted for Israel that on the festivals they read in the Torah on the subject of the festival, and likewise instituted for Israel "that they ask and expound on the subject of the day: the laws of Pesaḥ on Pesaḥ, the laws of Atzeret on Atzeret, the laws of the Ḥag on the Ḥag" (Megilla 32a; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 429:5). As the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe our teacher: Make for yourself great assemblies, and expound before them publicly on the subject of the day, so that the coming generations learn from you to gather assemblies every Shabbat and festival, and to gather in the houses of study to teach and instruct Israel words of Torah, the forbidden and the permitted, so that My great name be praised among My children (Yalkut Shimoni, Vayak'hel 408). And so the Sages of Israel acted throughout all the generations, expounding before the public in halakha and aggada. The central derasha took place during the day and was called 'Pirka', and they were very careful that everyone come to hear it (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:4, and in the Harḥavot there). On the nights of Sabbaths and festivals too they would set a derasha, and apparently they would engage in it mostly in aggada (Mordekhai, Pesaḥim 611), and women too would come to hear it (Yerushalmi Sota 1:4).

The Sages said that one must divide the time of Shabbat and the festival: half of it for God in Torah study in the beit midrash, and half of it for the delight of Shabbat with eating, drinking and sleeping (Pesaḥim 68b). When one subtracts the seven hours that a person needs to sleep at night, about eighteen hours remain, half of which, that is, nine hours, one must devote to God in Torah study. Indeed, since prayer too contains parts of Torah, and one can say that it too is part of the half that is devoted to God, one can count three of the nine hours for prayer; but at least six hours must be devoted to Torah study (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:1).

[Video]

sections.title_en: The Mitzva to Remember One's Learning
sections.body_en:
An important foundation in the mitzva of Torah study is that the goal is to know and remember what one learns. Some mistakenly think that the main thing is to understand what one learns at the time of study, but that afterwards there is no need to review the learning in order to remember it. But the truth is that the main thing is to know the Torah. And so the Sages said (Kiddushin 30a): "'And you shall teach them diligently (ve-shinantam)' – that the words of Torah be sharp in your mouth, so that if a person asks you something, do not stammer and tell him, but tell him immediately." That is, the mitzva is to understand and remember the words of the Torah (as explained in note 1). In this way every person will be able to fulfil the mitzvot of the Torah properly. In addition, it is a great merit for a person that the words of Torah, which are the words of the living God, rest in his memory, for through this he cleaves to the Torah and to the Giver of the Torah, and his whole life is elevated and sanctified and receives inspiration and guidance from the words of the Torah.

The Sages said: "Whoever forgets one thing of his learning, Scripture regards him as though he were liable for his life." For he knowingly loses words of the living God. But if he forgot under duress, because he was busy with his work and was not free for his study, he is not liable for his life. But when he is able, he must review his learning (Avot 3:8). And so it is cited in tractate Sanhedrin (99a): "Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa says: Whoever studies Torah and does not review it is like a person who sows and does not reap. Rabbi Yehoshua says: Whoever studies Torah and forgets it is like a woman who gives birth and buries." And some say that one who forgets one of the foundations of the Torah because he was negligent and did not make an effort to remember it transgresses a Torah prohibition, as it is said (Devarim 4:9): "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things" (Menaḥot 99b).

However, there is a difference between the period in which it was forbidden to write down the words of the Oral Torah – when there was an absolute obligation to remember the Oral Torah, for otherwise there was no way to go back and recall them – and today. Today, when it is permitted to write down the words of the Oral Torah, and not only that, but thanks to printing and the various databases one can easily recall every matter of Torah and halakha, the obligation is to remember the foundations of the Torah needed for the guidance of everyday life, and only if one forgets those does one transgress the prohibition of forgetting.5

Frequent reviews of one's learning express the learner's attachment to the words of the Torah. It is known that the Gra would test his students according to their attitude to reviewing. Any student whom he saw was bored by reviewing – he knew would not succeed in becoming a great Torah scholar. And anyone whose desire and joy in study grew with every additional review – he knew was capable of reaching high attainments in study.

[Video]

notes_en.en: According to Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 2:4, even at a time when books are available and through them one can recall what was forgotten, the prohibition against forgetting remains in its full force. But according to R. Ḥayim of Volozhin, these words were said about the early ones who studied by heart (Keter Rosh 67). And so wrote R. Avraham David of Buczacz in Divrei David on Avot 3:8. See also the book Be-Torato Yehgeh, chapter 10. But it seems that according to all opinions there is a mitzva to review much in order to connect to the words of the Torah and to know how to fulfil its mitzvot.

sections.body_en:
The uniqueness of the mitzva of Torah study is that it is a constant mitzva, and a person can never say: I have finished studying Torah, since there is no end to the ideas hidden in the Torah. In addition, the purpose of study is not only to know how to conduct oneself and how to look at the world; rather, study itself is considered the most exalted mitzva, for in Torah study we engage in the word of God that appears in the world, and there is no mitzva that connects a person to God more than the mitzva of Torah study, for the words of the divine Torah are absorbed into the mind of the learner and become part of him, and accordingly direct his life.

The basic difference between the mitzva of Torah study and the other mitzvot is that the Torah is connected to the eternal world of the spirit, and therefore the mitzva of study continues always, whereas the practical mitzvot are connected to the limited physical world, and therefore their fulfilment depends on time, place and person. For example, the mitzvot of the festivals and prayers depend on times. One cannot celebrate Pesaḥ in the middle of winter, and one cannot put on tefillin on Shabbat or at night. Likewise there are mitzvot that depend on place, such as the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot, which is fulfilled only in the Land of Israel, and by a person who grows grain or fruit. And likewise many mitzvot between man and his fellow depend on the person, for not everyone merits to meet a person in need of kindness every day. Likewise a poor person cannot fulfil the mitzva of tzedaka properly. And there are mitzvot that are specific to kohanim, and some that are specific to Yisraelim.

But the mitzva of Torah study, precisely because it represents the world of eternity, applies equally to all, and therefore Yisraelim too have a mitzva to study the laws of the kohanim, and even one who has no field is commanded to study the laws of one who has a field. And since the mitzva of Torah study represents the world of eternity, it continues all the time, by day and by night, from the time a person is young until his last day, as it is said (Yehoshua 1:8): "And you shall meditate on it day and night." And as the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:10): "Until when is one obligated to study Torah? Until the day of his death, as it is said (Devarim 4:9): 'And lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.' And whenever he does not engage in study, he forgets."

The Rambam further wrote (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:8): "Every man of Israel is obligated in Torah study, whether poor or rich, whether whole in body or afflicted with suffering, whether young or a very old man whose strength has waned; even a poor man who goes begging from door to door, and even one with a wife and children, is obligated to set himself a time for Torah study by day and by night, as it is said: And you shall meditate on it day and night."

[Video]

sections.title_en: The Merit of the Crown of Torah
sections.body_en:
The Sages said: "With three crowns Israel were crowned." The crown is a symbol of honour, and there are three kinds of honoured people among the people of Israel. Of the three crowns, two pass by inheritance, and one crown is acquired through a person's effort, and it is precisely this crown that is the most important of all. The three crowns are: "the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood and the crown of kingship. The crown of priesthood was attained by Aharon, as it is said (Bamidbar 25:13): 'And it shall be for him and for his descendants after him a covenant of everlasting priesthood.' The crown of kingship was attained by David, as it is said (Tehillim 89:37): 'His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before Me.' The crown of Torah lies ready and waiting for all of Israel, as it is said (Devarim 33:4): 'Moshe commanded us a Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Ya'akov' – whoever wishes may come and take it. Lest you say that those crowns are greater than the crown of Torah, Scripture says (Mishlei 8:15-16): 'By me kings reign and princes decree justice; by me rulers rule' – thus you have learned that the crown of Torah is greater than both of them" (Rambam, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:1, based on Yoma 72b).

There is halakhic significance to the fact that the crown of Torah is more important than the other crowns. For example, when several poor people are in need of tzedaka to an equal degree, and there is not enough in the fund to support all of them, a kohen takes precedence over a Levi, a Levi over a Yisrael, and a Yisrael over a mamzer. When is this said? When they are equal in wisdom; but if there was a mamzer who is a Torah scholar and a high priest who is an ignoramus, the mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence (SA YD 251:9).

Indeed it is a wondrous fact in Israel that there is no standing more honoured than the standing of the great Torah scholars, and all of Israel can belong to this standing, and many times the children of the poor merited to rise in Torah until they became the great ones of Israel. Behold Rabbi Akiva, who was poor and the son of converts, merited to be one of the great ones of Israel of all the generations. And likewise Hillel the Elder, who was desperately poor and studied Torah with self-sacrifice, rose and was appointed Nasi of Israel.

[Video]

The Torah is not like the natural sciences, which one can study and understand without special inner preparation; rather, the Torah is the word of God, and therefore without suitable preparation it is impossible to absorb it properly in the mind and the heart. The preparations are good character traits. A person who has not corrected his character traits will not be able to understand the Torah of God properly. The good character traits of Israel are the foundation for their being chosen from all the nations to receive the Torah. This is what the Sages said (Yevamot 79a): "There are three signs in this nation: they are compassionate, bashful (in the sense of fearing Heaven), and performers of kindness."

Of all the bad character traits, all of which hinder and harm study, there is no trait as harmful as the trait of pride. The words of Torah were compared to water, as it is said (Yeshayahu 55:1): "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the water", to teach us that it gives life to the world like water, and to tell us that just as water flows and trickles down to a low place, so the Torah is not absorbed in the minds of the arrogant and the proud. Rather, only one who is humble and modest can absorb the divine Torah (Ta'anit 7a).

Also one who is sunk in physical desires or the desire for money cannot rise and connect properly to the divine Torah. Therefore one who wishes to grow great in Torah and to be crowned with the crown of Torah should not divert his mind to other things, should not be drawn after desires, and should not seek to acquire Torah together with wealth and honour. Rather, he should devote his life to the study of Torah, and even if for this he must eat bread with salt, drink water by measure and sleep on the ground, he should continue to toil in Torah. For only one who is prepared to devote himself with all his strength to Torah study can merit it (see Rambam, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:6).

[Video]

sections.title_en: The Attitude of Halakha to Secular Studies
sections.body_en:
The most important study for a person is the study of Torah, through which a person reveals his divine soul, corrects his character traits and understands his destiny. The question is what the place of secular studies is.

The basic difference between Torah study and the study of external wisdoms is that the study of external wisdoms is intended mainly as a means to another end. For example, one studies physics or electronics in order to use the fruits of science to improve the conditions of human life. Therefore there is no need for all human beings to specialise in every single field of science; it is enough that there be sufficient scientists who can refine and develop science. But Torah study is an end in itself. Through the Torah and its guidance a person corrects himself, so that he will be able to master the negative sides of his character, and to direct his positive sides towards the highest aim of repairing the world under the kingship of the Almighty. Moreover, Torah study reveals the divine soul hidden in man. Therefore every Jew is obligated to engage in Torah every day.

At the same time, after emphasising the value of Torah study, which is more exalted than all the wisdoms, one must know that there is also value in general knowledge of the secular sciences. The Maharal of Prague in Netiv Ha-Torah (chapter 14) explains that wisdom in general is the most exalted divine revelation in the world, as it is said (Mishlei 2:6): "For the Lord gives wisdom; out of His mouth come knowledge and understanding", that is, even the natural sciences and human wisdom have their root in divine wisdom. For the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world with wisdom, and science grasps part of the divine wisdom hidden in the world.

And so the Sages instituted that a special blessing be recited on seeing a great sage from among the sages of the nations of the world: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has given of His wisdom to flesh and blood" (Berakhot 58a; Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 15:18). That is, even the secular sciences are considered His wisdom, for in the text of the blessing we say "who has given of His wisdom". It is indeed clear that the Torah is sanctified and exalted above all wisdoms, and therefore a special blessing was instituted for one who sees the sages of Israel; but in any case we find that the secular wisdoms too are a branch of divine wisdom.

And so the Sages said (Shabbat 75a): "Whoever knows how to calculate the seasons and the constellations and does not calculate them – concerning him Scripture says (Yeshayahu 5:12): They do not regard the work of the Lord, nor have they seen the work of His hands." Calculating the seasons and constellations is calculating the course of the stars in the heavens. The Rambam, the Maharal and many of the great ones of Israel explain that the intention is not that only the wisdom of astronomy is important and worthy of study; rather, the intention is that whoever can understand with wisdom the order of created nature and does not understand it, ignores the work of God. It is further explained there in the Gemara that through Israel being expert in the external wisdoms, a sanctification of God's name is made in the eyes of the nations, as it is said (Devarim 4:6): "Keep therefore and do them, for this is your wisdom and your understanding in the eyes of the peoples."

Apparently one could ask: were we not commanded to study Torah by day and by night? If so, whenever we stop studying Torah and engage in external wisdoms, is there not apparently neglect of Torah in this? But engaging in wisdoms is not considered neglect of Torah. The Maharal brought a proof for this from Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, of whom it was said that he never neglected Torah in his days, and he engaged in the study of astronomy (Sukka 28a). And what Shmuel said, that he would study astrology only at the time when he was in the lavatory, when it is forbidden to study Torah (Devarim Rabba 8:6), refers to the art of foretelling the future by the stars, which is not considered a wisdom that precisely examines the order of nature but rather a kind of intuition and segula. And as for what they said in the Gemara (Bava Kamma 82b), that they decreed not to study Greek wisdom, the Rivash and the Maharal already explained that the intention is Greek manners and culture, and they did not forbid studying external wisdoms.

Likewise it is well known in the name of the Gaon of Vilna that he encouraged his students to study external wisdoms, and encouraged R. Barukh of Shklov to translate Euclid from Greek into Hebrew, so that the students could study geometry. And he told him that to the extent that a person lacks knowledge of the other wisdoms, he will correspondingly lack a hundredfold in the wisdom of the Torah, for the Torah and wisdom are bound together. And likewise Rav Yisrael of Shklov, in his introduction to his book 'Pe'at Ha-shulḥan', wrote in the name of the Gra that all the wisdoms are needed for our Torah, and testified that the Gra knew algebra, trigonometry and geometry well, and the science of music and all the other wisdoms. Only the art of making medicines he did not study, for his righteous father decreed upon him that he not study it, so that he would not neglect Torah when he would need to go to save lives. It follows, then, that there is great value in studying the wisdoms, and that this was the position of the Sages.

[Video]

sections.title_en: The Problem of Secular Studies in the Period of Exile
sections.body_en:
In the period of the Rishonim (about eight hundred years ago) a serious problem began to arise around the study of the external wisdoms. Most books of science were based on the opinions of Aristotle and the sages of ancient Greece, and together with the words of science they absorbed words of heresy concerning the creation of the world, individual providence, and reward and punishment. And there were Jewish youths who, following study in the various secular books, were also drawn after the outlooks of their authors, until they left their religion and their people and assimilated.

Therefore, despite the great value of studying the various wisdoms, many of the great ones of Israel kept young men away from studying them. The Rashba, who was the leader of Spanish Jewry in his generation, together with his beit din, imposed a ḥerem and a prohibition on anyone who would study the Greek books of science before the age of twenty-five, and likewise on the teachers who would teach young students who had not yet reached the age of twenty-five (Responsa Rashba 1:414).

And there were rabbis who wrote that it is fitting not to study the books of Aristotle at all, for with all the importance of the external wisdoms, if studying them is liable to cause distancing from faith in God and from the words of the divine Torah that we received at Sinai, their entire value is null and void, and it is better not to study them at all (Responsa Rivash 45).

And so the Maharal of Prague wrote (Netiv Ha-Torah 14), that although there is great value in studying the wisdoms and sciences, it is forbidden to study them from books in which words of heresy are absorbed. Only if the learner intends to study them in order to know what to answer the apikorsim is he permitted to study them.

About two hundred years ago this problem grew more acute. On the one hand, the books of science were no longer based on the philosophical conception of Aristotle; but on the other hand, the Haskala that developed in Europe began to draw after it many Jews, who thought to themselves: here, science will come and solve all of humanity's problems, and there is no longer any need for Torah and mitzvot. And so it happened that many of the Jews of Western Europe who studied external wisdoms left the way of Israel of old and converted.

The counter-reaction of some of the great ones of Israel was to forbid secular studies with greater force. But this prohibition too did not stand in the breach, and most of the Jewish public was drawn after the Haskala, abandoned Torah study and weakened in the observance of mitzvot.

But the Gaon of Vilna held that one should encourage the Torah scholars of Israel to study secular studies, and on the contrary, precisely through this it would be possible to grow great in Torah and sanctify God's name in the eyes of the nations, and to prevent the young men of Israel from being drawn after foreign cultures. And so Rabbi Hillel of Shklov wrote about the Gra: "It is well known that our master… engaged much also in researching the properties of nature, the studies of the earth, for the sake of attaining the wisdom of the Torah, for the sake of sanctifying God's name in the eyes of the nations, and for the sake of bringing the redemption closer. Already from his youth he showed wonders in all seven wisdoms and sought much. He also commanded his students to study as much as possible of the seven wisdoms of the studies of the earth, also in order to raise the wisdom of Israel according to the wisdom of the Torah in the eyes of the nations… And from mouth to ear he told us many times: What are our Torah scholars doing for the sanctification of the Name, as the early ones among the great of Israel did, many of whom sanctified the name of Heaven through their great knowledge in researching the secrets of nature, the wonders of the Creator, blessed be His name, so that many of the pious of the nations also extolled the wisdom of Israel, the sages of the Torah, the men of the Sanhedrin, Tannaim and Amoraim, etc., and in later generations our master the Rambam, the author of the 'Tosafot Yom Tov' and others, who greatly sanctified the name of Heaven in the eyes of the gentiles through their wisdom in the studies of the earth" (Kol Ha-tor 5:2).

Also among the rabbis in Germany, who saw from close up the spiritual disaster that befell the Jewish communities because of being drawn after the Haskala, an educational approach took shape that was called "Torah im Derekh Eretz". Instead of banning secular studies, they encouraged yeshiva students to study secular studies in a controlled manner, in order to immunise them against the mistaken conception that secular education can replace the Torah.

And although all the great ones of Israel agree that there is value in studying external wisdoms, in practice the debate continues. Some hold that secular studies are liable to cause abandonment of religion, and some hold that, on the contrary, introducing secular studies into the order of study in yeshivot at high-school age will prevent the young men from being swept after secular education, and will broaden their minds in understanding the Torah, as the Gaon of Vilna said.6

In practice, regrettably, if we survey the last hundred years, we will find that many abandoned the mitzvot in both streams, and it is difficult to determine from which more left. In any case, I will not refrain from stating my opinion. It is precisely the approach that includes secular studies that is more correct for the many. First, because in truth there is value in studying external wisdoms, both from the aspect of recognising the greatness of God, as explained in the Gemara in tractate Shabbat (75a) and in the words of the Rambam, the Maharal, the Gra and many others; and from the aspect of sanctifying God's name in the eyes of the nations; and from the economic aspect, for graduates of the yeshiva high schools, thanks to their general education, can acquire a prestigious profession, support their families respectably, and attain an honoured standing in the eyes of people.

In addition, it seems that this approach is more successful for preserving Judaism. And although not a few of the graduates of the yeshiva high schools abandoned the observance of mitzvot, this is not because they studied secular studies, but generally because their parents' home too was far from observance of mitzvot at a proper level. By contrast, from those yeshiva high schools that educate properly for fear of Heaven and faith while emphasising the supremacy of sacred studies, with the backing of the parents' home, the number of graduates who abandoned the Torah was small relative to all the other yeshivot.

Of course one must add that the issue of abandoning the observance of mitzvot, or returning to the observance of mitzvot, cannot be examined only on the scale of studying or not studying secular studies. Anyone who wishes to deal with this issue seriously must take into account many factors, among them: historical and social processes, the crises and upheavals that the Jewish people underwent in the modern period, and more.

notes_en.en: What I wrote, that all agree that there is value in the study of the sciences, refers to what the great Rishonim and Aḥaronim wrote. Indeed, in recent generations there were among the great ones of Israel those who taught that it is preferable to study in a yeshiva that does not combine secular studies, for the reason that it is desirable to devote all one's time to Torah and not to things of lower value than Torah. And so it is written in Igrot Moshe YD 3:81-82. And so it is written in Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:75; 5:56. Indeed, according to those who reject secular studies, there is added the concern that people will be drawn too far after them. But on the other hand Rav Kook, in Orot Ha-Torah 9:4, wrote that there is value in every Torah scholar being versed to some extent in general science, and so he wrote in Ikvei Ha-tzon, p. 129, and as we cited above, its source is in the holy one of Israel, the pious Gaon of Vilna.

sections.body_en:
There is a difference in the obligation of the mitzva of Torah study between men and women. The obligation incumbent upon women is to study Torah in order to know its guidance for life; for this purpose every woman is obligated to study halakha, faith and ethics. And a woman who has studied and knows the practical laws, and the foundations of faith and ethics at a level and depth that satisfy her desire and quench her thirst, is not obligated to study further. But a man who has studied and knows everything needed for the guidance of his life according to the Torah is obligated to continue studying and delving further into the Torah.

In other words, there are two parts to study. One is knowing the guidance of the Torah in order to live a complete life, and this is the part in which men and women are equally obligated. The second part is that which tends towards inquiry, pilpul and research, and in it men are obligated and not women. Therefore there is a difference between the yeshivot in which boys study and the ulpanot in which girls study. In the yeshivot they engage much in the study of Gemara, in which the theoretical side is prominent. And in the ulpanot they teach halakha, Tanakh, thought and ethics, which are the studies that belong more to the guidance of life.

And although a woman who has studied everything needed for the guidance of her life according to the Torah is not obligated to study further, it is a mitzva for her to broaden and deepen the study of halakha, faith and ethics, in order to cleave more to God, to His Torah and His mitzvot. And there were famous women in Israel who were known as Torah scholars of great stature. And if she wishes, she may also study Gemara in depth, delving into the various approaches and the variant readings. The Sages even said that if she does so she has fulfilled a mitzva and has merit, even though she is not obligated in it.

But for women who have no special desire to delve into the Torah, the general guidance is not to go deeply into the pilpul of the approaches, but to study clearly the summary of the practical laws with their reasons, and the foundations of faith and ethics.

There were generations in which women fulfilled the obligation of their study by a very simple study of laws connected to the home and the family and a few words of ethics, because this study was enough to create in their souls the desired identification and devotion to the observance of the Torah and Jewish life. But in recent generations, with the development of general education and the professional specialisation of women in various fields, it is clear that women must study much more Torah than they studied in the past, both because of the growing and broadening interest in general questions and because of the responsibility placed upon women. Indeed, according to the guidance of the great ones of Israel, already several generations ago educational institutions and institutions of Torah study at a high level were established especially for girls and women, such as the 'Beit Ya'akov' institutions that were founded by Mrs Sarah Schenirer with the encouragement and support of the great rabbis of Poland before the Second World War.

As the years pass, knowledge and wisdom become the possession of the broad public, and the challenges of life demand a higher Torah level, and accordingly the obligation of women to delve into Torah study, halakha, faith and ethics keeps broadening, and the gap between the obligation of men and the obligation of women narrows – until even in the educational institutions for boys, because of the investment in the study of Gemara, which does not reach the halakhic conclusions, and the foundations of faith and ethics, they find it hard to fulfil all the study that women are obligated to study, and all the more so in the educational institutions for girls they do not fulfil it.

This change, which narrowed the difference between the obligation of women and the obligation of men, does not nullify the difference in principle between men, who are obligated in Torah study also for the sake of the research and theoretical side, and women, who are not obligated in this, and only a woman who wishes to fulfils a mitzva. Rav Kook explains that it is precisely through this difference between men and women that a complementarity is created between the analysing and obligating intellect and the natural feeling that unites and establishes the words of the Torah in real life (see Peninei Halakha, 'Women's Prayer' chapter 3, and 'Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato' chapter 10, on what is equal, what is different and what is mutually enriching between men and women; and see the commentary Ein Aya on tractate Berakhot, chapter 7, 46).7
