Sota 20a: according to Ben Azzai it is a mitzva for a father to teach his daughter Torah. Whereas according to Rabbi Eliezer it is forbidden to teach her, for whoever teaches his daughter Torah is as though he teaches her frivolity. Rabbi Yehoshua also agrees with him. And in the Yerushalmi, Sota 3:4, it is explained that according to R. Elazar ben Azarya there is indeed a mitzva that women hear the Torah, but there is no mitzva that they study it in depth. In practice the Rambam ruled in Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:13 like Rabbi Eliezer, that one should not teach a daughter Torah, because most women's minds are not directed to it, and if he teaches her the Oral Torah it is as though he teaches her frivolity. The Written Torah too one should not teach her, but in any case if he taught her he is not considered as teaching her frivolity. And so wrote the Tur and SA YD 246:6. The difference between the Written Torah and the Oral Torah is that we learned that the Written Torah is commanded to be heard at 'Hakhel', and from this it follows that it is not considered frivolity.
But one who wishes to study without being obligated to do so may study and has merit in it, as explained in the Rambam there: "A woman who studied Torah has a reward, but it is not like the reward of a man, because she was not commanded, and whoever does something that he is not commanded to do, his reward is not like the reward of one who is commanded and does it, but less than it. And although she has a reward, the Sages commanded that a person not teach his daughter Torah, because most women's minds are not directed to being taught, but they turn words of Torah into words of nonsense according to the poverty of their understanding. The Sages said: whoever teaches his daughter Torah is as though he taught her frivolity. When is this said? Regarding the Oral Torah; but the Written Torah he should not teach her ab initio, and if he taught her, it is not like teaching her frivolity." That is, since generally girls did not have the leisure and desire to delve properly, they studied partially, and this led them to mistaken understandings and words of frivolity. But if she herself is interested in this, and is prepared to invest the time and inquiry required in order to understand properly, she has merit in it. And so it is explained in the Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 4:14, that there is a mitzva for every person to love God and fear Him, and the way to arrive at His love and fear in completeness is through the study of Torah, at first in the discussions of Abaye and Rava, in knowing the permitted and the forbidden in all the mitzvot, and afterwards in Ma'aseh Bereshit and Merkava. And the Rambam wrote about this: "For they are the great good that the Holy One, blessed be He, bestowed for the settlement of this world in order to inherit the World to Come, and it is possible for all to know them, great and small, man and woman, one with a broad heart and one with a narrow heart." (And so wrote Rav Rabinovitch in his commentary on the Rambam, 'Yad Peshuta'.) It follows that the ideal is that all women study the Torah in depth of their own will, and arrive at the love of God and His fear in completeness. And it is likewise known that there were prophetesses and women Torah scholars. Thus one whose soul desires theoretical study is commanded to study. That is, the difference between men and women is that women should engage in Torah out of freedom and will, as explained at length in Peninei Halakha, Women's Prayer, chapter 3.
All this is said regarding study for the sake of inquiry alone. But a woman is obligated to study the mitzvot that she must fulfil, and so wrote the Rema YD 246:6, based on the Agur in the name of the Semag. And likewise in SA OḤ 47:14 it was ruled that women recite the blessing of the Torah, and the reason is that they must study what they need in order to live according to the Torah. Today women must study halakha well, with its halakhic and conceptual reasons, and the foundations of faith and ethics, and without this their Torah life will certainly not be at a proper level; therefore it is an obligation to teach girls as much as is needed for the observance of the Torah and the establishment of faith.

sections.title_en: Rising in Honour of Torah Scholars
sections.body_en:
It is a Torah mitzva to honour Torah scholars, as it is said (Devarim 6:13): "The Lord your God you shall fear – to include Torah scholars" (Pesaḥim 22b). Included in the mitzva is rising in honour of a Torah scholar even if he is young, as it is said (Vayikra 19:32): "And you shall honour the face of the elder (zaken)" – "zaken means only one who has acquired wisdom" (Kiddushin 32b; Rambam, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 6:1). A Torah scholar is one who has studied Torah and understands life in its light, and teaches, guides and rules according to the Torah. But one who has studied, examined and analysed a great deal, but does not know how to educate, guide and rule on the questions of life, is not considered a Torah scholar (see Shakh 244:11).

The mitzva is that it be evident that the rising is in honour of the sage, and therefore the mitzva is to rise when the sage enters within his four cubits, until he passes in front of him (SA YD 244:2; 9). However, in honour of his principal teacher it is a mitzva to rise when he sees him from afar, as long as it is evident that he is rising in his honour, and to continue standing until he moves away or sits in his place (Ran, Kiddushin 33a; SA 244:9).

The mitzva of honour is to rise to one's full height (Tur; Taz 244:4; Ḥayei Adam 69:4). In practice, however, many customarily make do with showing 'hiddur' (a gesture of respect) to a Torah scholar, that is, they raise themselves a little as though beginning to rise in his honour. It seems that since the rabbis did not teach the students that they must rise to their full height in their honour, this implies that they agreed to it, and a rabbi who has waived his honour – his honour is waived (SA 244:14). However, in honour of his principal teacher one must rise to his full height until he reaches his place. Similarly, during the period in which one studies Torah from a rabbi, such as a rosh yeshiva for his students or a rabbi who gives a regular class, it is a mitzva for those who learn from him to rise fully in his honour within his four cubits. Likewise in honour of a local rabbi who spreads Torah in his community it is a mitzva to rise fully within his four cubits.

The poskim disagreed about the law of students who study with the rabbi in his home. Some say that they must rise before him every time he enters and leaves the room, even a hundred times (Rosh; Birkei Yosef 242:21). And some say that they must rise before him twice a day, morning and evening, so that the honour of the rabbi not be greater than the honour of Heaven (Rambam, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 6:8, based on Kiddushin 33b). However, even according to the lenient opinion, in a place that is not the rabbi's home, it is a mitzva to rise before him when he enters and when he leaves, for perhaps there are other people there who do not know that they already rose before him in the morning, or will rise before him when he leaves in the evening (Tosafot; Rema 242:16). And if during the same study session in the yeshiva, or during the same assembly, the rabbi goes out or comes in, according to the lenient opinion there is no need to rise before him, since everyone knows that they rose before him when he first entered and will rise before him when he leaves on his way. And so is the widespread custom, except in cases in which the rabbi goes up to give a class or to the Torah, or turns to speak with a person who is sitting, for then, although they rose before him when he entered, they rise before him again.

Two sages – one need not rise before the other, but should show him 'hiddur' (SA 244:8). Likewise, a rabbi need not rise before his student who is a sage, but it is good to show him hiddur (Rema, ibid.). However, it seems that it is proper to rise at a time when it is called for to rise before him, such as when he is about to give a class and everyone rises in his honour.

One who is engaged in his work, and rising would require him to interrupt his work, is not obligated to rise (SA 244:5). One does not stand in the lavatory or in the bathhouse, for there is no honour in rising there (ibid. 4). Also when engaged in Torah study it is a mitzva to rise (SA 244:11; Yad Rama, Kiddushin 33b). In the middle of a Torah class, there is no mitzva to rise before another rabbi who enters late, and sometimes this even involves an affront to the honour of the class and of the rabbi giving it.

It is fitting for Torah scholars not to trouble the public to rise in their honour, even if for this purpose they must lengthen their way (SA 244:6).

It is a mitzva to rise also before the wife of a Torah scholar, for the wife of a ḥaver is like a ḥaver. It seems that the intention is the rabbanit who is a full partner in assisting his study and in spreading Torah. Even if her husband has died, as long as she has not remarried, it is a mitzva to rise before her (Shevu'ot 30b; Rishonim there). Likewise, a rabbanit or a teacher who teaches Torah – it is a mitzva for her students to rise before her when she enters within their four cubits, and likewise it is a mitzva for all to rise when she enters to give them a class.
